title: A Spot on the Lung Found by Chance / Size, Risk and Growth Decide

blocks.text: A Spot on the Lung Found by Chance / Size, Risk and Growth Decide

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-35 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: British Thoracic Society guidelines for the investigation and management of pulmonary nodules (Thorax 2015;70 Suppl 2:ii1-ii54) · Related AMaC: AMaC incidental lung nodule station (same topic) and lobar collapse examination station

Dear Doctor, a 67-year-old retired bus mechanic. A CT scan of his chest and abdomen for back pain showed a 9 mm solid nodule in the right upper lobe. He smoked for 40 years and stopped ten years ago. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. A solid nodule of 8 mm or more in an older ex-smoker is a risk calculation, not a reassurance. The station turns on the size rule, the risk score and the growth rate, and on giving him the red flags.

The Examiner Trap. He hopes it is nothing. Candidates reassure and discharge, or rush to biopsy. Pass: size of 8 mm or more so Brock risk model; risk above 10% means PET-CT and a chest team; growth tells you more. Fail: discharged with no plan.

rows: Ask about cough, blood, weight loss and breathlessness, then smoking, asbestos, past cancer and family history.
"Any cough, blood, weight loss or breathlessness? When did you stop smoking? Any asbestos or past cancer?"
Cough; haemoptysis; weight loss; breathlessness; smoking; asbestos; cancer; family history; back pain.
Examine the chest and neck, the hands and the spine, and look for signs of spread.
"May I look at your hands, neck and chest, and press along your back? Tell me if anything hurts."
Clubbing; nodes; chest; spine tenderness; liver; weight; cover him.
Explain what the nodule is, why size and risk matter, what happens next and which symptoms are urgent.
"The nodule is bigger than the size we watch, so I'd like the lung team to see it. Come back quickly if you cough blood."
Risk score; repeat CT; PET; biopsy; growth rate; red flags; review.
No introduction or consent; examines without asking; leaves him exposed.
Introduces self, asks consent, asks about discomfort before examining, covers him and thanks him.
Also offers a chaperone and acknowledges how frightening a lung finding is.
Asks about smoking only; omits haemoptysis, weight loss, asbestos or past cancer.
Asks cough, haemoptysis, weight loss, breathlessness, smoking history, asbestos and past cancer.
Also asks about family history, previous chest imaging and why the CT was done.
Omits the nodes or spine; reports signs of lung cancer that are absent.
Finds no clubbing, no neck nodes, a clear chest, no spinal tenderness and no hepatomegaly.
Also records the weight loss he describes and the otherwise unremarkable examination.
Calls it harmless, or calls it cancer with no reasoning.
A solid nodule of 8 mm or more in an ex-smoker: indeterminate, with a malignant risk that must be calculated.
Also names infection, a benign hamartoma, metastasis and granuloma as other causes.
Asks for no follow-up, or for an immediate biopsy.
Says a nodule of 8 mm or more needs the Brock risk model; risk above 10% means PET-CT and chest team referral, where tissue is decided.

Also names volume doubling time: a volume change of 25% or more is real growth; under 400 days needs further investigation; 400 to 600 days means yearly scans or biopsy; over 600 days allows discharge or surveillance.
Says to return urgently with haemoptysis, new breathlessness or weight loss, and arranges a clear follow-up date.
Also advises him to stay stopped from smoking and offers a written summary.
Brushes aside his fear of cancer.
Asks what worries him, acknowledges it and explains that many nodules turn out benign.
Also discusses his wife and his plans.
Tells him what to do with no choices.
Explains the risk-based plan and asks his preferences about investigation.
Records his preferences, gives a written plan and a dated review.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 67-year-old retired bus mechanic. You are practical, a little anxious and hoping for good news.
Opening line: "They said they found a spot on my lung while looking at my back. I feel fine, so I'm sure it's nothing."
Volunteered: you smoked about 20 a day for 40 years and stopped ten years ago.

Only if asked: a slight morning cough for a year. No blood. You have lost a little weight without trying. You worked near asbestos lagging years ago. You take amlodipine for blood pressure; no allergies; you drink little alcohol; no recent travel; you live with your wife.
Only if asked about family: your brother died of lung cancer at 70.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid you have the same cancer as your brother. Say: "He went downhill in months."
Your questions, in your own words: "Is it cancer?" "Do I need a biopsy?" "How long will it take?"
How you react: if falsely reassured, you leave worried. If listened to and given a clear plan, you engage. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable; respiratory rate 14; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 132/78; SpO2 96% on air; temperature 36.6 °C. Thin; weight 4 kg lower than a year ago. No clubbing. No neck nodes. Chest clear. No spinal tenderness. No hepatomegaly.

Results, only when requested: CT (dedicated chest): solid 9 mm nodule right upper lobe, spiculated edge; no other nodules. Risk model: above 10%. Repeat CT at 3 months, if done: volume increase of 40%.

Question ladder: 1. What do you do with a nodule of 8 mm or more? (E) 2. What does a risk above 10% mean? (E) 3. What does a volume doubling time under 400 days mean? (E) 4. When can a nodule be discharged? (E) 5. Which symptoms are red flags? (E)

Curveballs: He asks for a quick biopsy: not before the team has planned it. He asks why not just repeat the scan in a year: the size and risk need earlier assessment. He coughs up blood: urgent review.
Introduces self, asks consent and asks about discomfort before examining (G)
Asks about haemoptysis, weight loss, asbestos and past cancer (C)
Examines hands, neck nodes, chest and spine (A)
Finds no clubbing, nodes or spinal tenderness (B)
Names an indeterminate solid nodule of 8 mm or more with malignant risk (D)
Says use a risk model or refer to a chest team (E)
Says a risk above 10% means chest referral (E)
Uses volume doubling time and growth in the plan (E)
Gives red flags and a follow-up date (E)
Asks what worries him and addresses his brother's death (F)
Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Take your shirt off. [R1 Fail] Do you cough? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the nodes and spine.) [R3 Fail] It's nothing. [R4 Fail] Nothing more is needed. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: You can go home and forget about it. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] No review. [R8 Fail]
Examiner note: No consent, no examination, a risky nodule dismissed, and no warning symptoms given.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I look at your hands, neck and chest and press along your back? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Any cough with blood or weight loss? Any asbestos? Any past cancer? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: A morning cough, some weight loss, and asbestos years ago.
CANDIDATE: (Examines, then covers him.) No clubbing, no nodes, a clear chest, a pain-free spine and no liver edge. Thank you for letting me examine you. [R3 Pass] [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: A solid nodule of 8 mm or more in an ex-smoker is indeterminate; the risk needs calculating. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: A nodule of 8 mm or more needs the Brock risk calculation. A risk above 10% means a PET-CT and referral to the chest team, who decide on tissue. [R5 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Come back at once if you cough blood or become breathless. I'll book your review today. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: I'm afraid it's what my brother had.
CANDIDATE: That is a fair fear; many nodules are benign. [R7 Pass] Shall we arrange the chest clinic this week? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Used the size rule, the risk threshold and safety-netting. Did not name other causes, volume doubling time, or a written plan.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? A lung finding is frightening. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any family history or earlier chest scans? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Weight is down a little; the examination is otherwise normal. [R3 High]
CANDIDATE: Infection, a hamartoma, a granuloma and metastasis are other causes. [R4 High]

CANDIDATE: A volume change of 25% or more is real growth. A doubling time under 400 days needs further investigation; 400 to 600 days: consider yearly scans or a biopsy; over 600 days: consider discharge or ongoing scans. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Stay off cigarettes, and I'll give you a written summary. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: We'll talk with your wife if you'd like. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a review date. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, other causes, volume doubling time, smoking advice and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about haemoptysis and weight loss. They raise the risk.
R4: Calling it nothing. A solid nodule of 8 mm or more in an ex-smoker is indeterminate.
R5: Skipping the risk and referral step. Size of 8 mm or more needs the risk model or a chest team.
R6: Giving no warning symptoms. Red flags need an urgent route.
"Can I ask about any coughing up of blood or weight loss?"
"A nodule of 8 mm or more needs a risk calculation."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

BTS 2015: solid nodules under 5 mm or under 80 mm3 need no follow-up; 5 mm to under 8 mm (80 to under 300 mm3) have CT surveillance; 8 mm or more (300 mm3 or more) need the Brock model (full version, with spiculation). Brock risk below 10%: CT surveillance; above 10%: offer PET-CT, then recalculate the risk with the Herder model (which includes PET uptake). Herder risk below 10%: surveillance; 10 to 70%: consider image-guided biopsy; above 70%: surgical resection is favoured.

At least a 25% change in volume is needed to count as growth. Stable at 1 year (under 25% volume change on semi-automated volumetry): discharge; if only diameter measurements are used, rescan at 2 years before discharge. Volume doubling time under 400 days: further diagnostic investigation; 400 to 600 days: consider yearly surveillance or biopsy; over 600 days: consider discharge or surveillance. Benign features (popcorn calcification) allow dismissal. A perifissural or subpleural nodule can be dismissed only if it is homogeneous, smooth, solid, lentiform or triangular, within 1 cm of the fissure or pleura, and under 10 mm.
A nodule of 8 mm or more is risk-stratified with the Brock model. Above 10% he goes for PET-CT and the lung cancer team, who decide on biopsy and treatment; below 10% he has CT surveillance.
THINK: Solid nodule of 8 mm or more in an ex-smoker: risk.
SAY: "I'd like the lung team to assess it."
DO: Ask haemoptysis, weight loss; examine nodes and spine.
NUMBERS: 8 mm; Brock risk 10% (PET-CT above it, then Herder); doubling time 400 and 600 days; growth 25% (BTS 2015).
TRAP: Reassured and discharged.
FINISH: Risk model, PET-CT, chest team, red flags, written plan.

Callister MEJ et al. British Thoracic Society guidelines for the investigation and management of pulmonary nodules. Thorax 2015;70(Suppl 2):ii1-ii54. https://thorax.bmj.com/content/70/Suppl_2/ii1 Supports: size thresholds, Brock model, PET-CT, volume doubling time and discharge criteria.
